sections.h2: Barron County housing and who collects
sections.html: Barron County is in northwestern Wisconsin, with the city of Barron as county seat. The 2020 census counted 46,711 residents, about 78 percent of them in rural areas, and 73.2 percent of occupied homes were owner-occupied. The cities are Barron, Chetek, Cumberland and Rice Lake. The villages are Almena, Cameron, Dallas, Haugen, New Auburn, Prairie Farm and Turtle Lake. Each of those places, and each surrounding town, has its own treasurer who takes first-installment payments.

sections.h2: Which Barron County office handles my property tax?
sections.html:
The county office to know is the Barron County Treasurer and Real Property Lister, at 335 E Monroe Ave, Room 2412, Barron, WI 54812-1478. Weekday hours run 8 a.m. until 4:30 p.m., and callers reach the staff at 715-537-6280. The Real Property Lister side maintains the parcel descriptions behind the assessment and tax roll, drawing on records from the Register of Deeds, surveying, zoning and mapping, the assessor and the treasurer. The office also hosts the online tax data portal.

The dates come from state law. Wis. Stat. 74.11 gives you a choice between one full payment and two equal installments, due January 31 and July 31. A parcel with a total bill under $100 is paid whole by January 31. Payments on or before January 31 are sent to the town, village or city treasurer, and the county treasurer takes everything later. Assessment is local in Wisconsin, so your municipal clerk can tell you who assessed your parcel and when the local Board of Review meets.

Interest and penalty are counted back to February 1. The county posts the rate as 1 percent interest plus a half percent penalty each month, 1.5 percent in all, in line with the interest authority in Wis. Stat. 74.47. The county gives 10.5 percent as the August charge on 2025 taxes still unpaid after the July 31, 2026 installment date. Taxes for 2025 come due in 2026 because they follow the prior year's assessment.

Miss the first installment and the full unpaid balance is delinquent from February 1. Mail timing deserves attention:

  • The postmark on a mailed check must be dated no later than the due date.
  • Local mail is often postmarked in Saint Paul, Minnesota, sometimes days later, so carry the envelope to the local post office and ask for a hand stamp.
  • An envelope that arrives with no postmark cannot be treated as timely.

Counties and municipalities can also sue an owner to recover delinquent taxes that came due while that person owned the property. This normally follows approval by the county board or governing body, and it is limited to the amount owed plus interest and penalties.

sections.h2: What a Barron County tax bill shows, and when it arrives
sections.html:
State law has the bill mailed by the third Monday in December. If it never arrives, what you owe and the collection of delinquent tax stay the same. The bill lists the tax from each taxing jurisdiction for the previous and current year with the percentage change, shows the school district tax net of the state credit, includes a notice of available credits, and says whether delinquent taxes or special assessments are attached to the parcel.

Read that last line before you list a house. It is the quickest way to spot a past-due amount. These bill requirements come from Wis. Stat. 74.09, next to the payment rules in chapter 74.

sections.h2: How can I pay Barron County property tax?
sections.html:
The treasurer takes four kinds of payment, and the taxpayer covers card and electronic fees.

One online or phone transaction can cover up to 15 parcels. Wait for the confirmation number before you assume the payment went through.

sections.h2: Deadlines for Barron County owners and sellers
sections.html:
A few small dates cause most of the grief.

  • January 15, land divisions. When a property was split into two or more parcels, the tax roll still shows the land as it stood on January 1. A new owner who wants the bill split for the part they bought must ask the town, village or city treasurer in writing by January 15.
  • January 31, first installment. Pay in full or pay the first half, to the municipal treasurer, to avoid interest and penalty.
  • January 31, lottery and gaming credit. The credit applies to owner-occupied primary residences. If it is missing from your statement and you qualify, file a late claim with the municipal treasurer by this date.
  • July 31, second installment. A late payment adds charges retroactive to February 1.

Assessment objections run on a different clock. Anyone planning to object must give notice at least 48 hours before the Board of Review first meets, then file the written objection in the opening two hours of that meeting. A changed-assessment notice has to be in the mail 15 days ahead of the board meeting, or 30 days ahead when the municipality revalues. Your municipal clerk posts the meeting date.

sections.h2: What a Barron County seller owes at closing
sections.html:
On a sale the seller owes Wisconsin's transfer fee of 30 cents for every $100 of value, and the register of deeds takes it at recording. The grantor and grantee both sign an electronic transfer return first. The fee comes from Wis. Stat. 77.22, and exemptions in section 77.25 cover cases such as conveyances by will or descent, foreclosure deeds, deeds in lieu of foreclosure to the lender and transfers between a parent and child for little or no payment. A conveyance claiming an exemption must state the reason on its face.

Property tax is its own matter. Request a statement of any delinquent amount from the Barron County Treasurer. Separately, ask the title company how the current year will be divided between you and the buyer. Paying the delinquent amount with interest and any penalty clears the debt, provided no tax certificate has yet been issued. Because first-installment payments go to the municipal treasurer, confirm with that treasurer which installment has been paid.

A short checklist keeps a Barron County closing from stalling on tax paperwork.

  • Find the tax bill and check its last line for delinquent taxes or special assessments.
  • Learn which municipal treasurer took your January payment and whether the second installment is paid.
  • Call 715-537-6280 for a statement of any delinquent amount.
  • If you claim a transfer fee exemption, have the reason ready for the face of the deed.
  • If land was divided during the year, ask the municipal treasurer about a bill split before January 15.

Cash buyers often close faster since no lender underwriting is involved. The transfer return and the tax payoff still apply, so build both into your timeline.

faqs.q: When are Barron County property taxes due?
faqs.a: The first installment, or the entire bill, is due January 31, and the second installment July 31. A bill under $100 is paid whole by January 31. Money paid on or before that date goes to the local municipal treasurer.

faqs.q: What interest applies to late Barron County taxes?
faqs.a: Each month costs 1.5 percent, counted from February 1: one percent in interest and half a percent in penalty. The county gives 10.5 percent as the August figure for 2025 taxes.

faqs.q: How do I contact the Barron County Treasurer?
faqs.a: Call 715-537-6280 or visit Room 2412 at 335 E Monroe Ave in Barron, weekdays between 8 a.m. and 4:30 p.m. Mail goes to Barron County Treasurer's Office, 335 E Monroe Ave Rm 2412, Barron, WI 54812-1478.

faqs.q: Who covers the transfer fee on a Barron County sale?
faqs.a: The seller. Sellers pay 30 cents per $100 of value, and the register of deeds takes the money at recording. Inheritance transfers, foreclosure deeds and certain family transfers for little or no payment are exempt.

faqs.q: What if my lottery credit is missing from my Barron County tax bill?
faqs.a: Ask your municipal treasurer to take a late claim, which must be in by January 31. Only an owner-occupied primary residence qualifies, and the Treasurer's Office can answer questions about eligibility.
